prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a concrete invention with a clear before and after: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping removes Doppler and recoil shifts for many atoms at once, and Ye's group took the approach to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and used the many-atom ensemble for new physics. It is reproduced and surpassed by independent laboratories, underpins the coming redefinition of the second, and gives centimetre-scale tests of time dilation and sensitive searches for varying constants and dark matter. Four colleagues who rank it first (Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth) or second (Pearce) give it the broadest and most scientifically independent support on the shortlist, and the two-name credit is the cleanest attribution of any shortlisted ballot. I moved it ahead of my own first-ranked circuit QED ballot, partly for the reasons in the case against and conflict note below.
statement.case_against: The clock is primarily an instrument and metrology achievement built on the frequency-comb and laser-cooling prizes of 2005 and 1997/2001, and some members may see it as an incremental precision gain rather than a discovery of a new phenomenon. Credit is also not fully exhaustive, since ion-clock groups and ultrastable-laser developers made essential contributions. Against my own earlier first choice, circuit QED is conceptually deeper for quantum information, but it sits very close in subject and time to the 2025 prize and its credit omits Girvin and others.

responses.point: B027 is a concrete invention that redefined frequency metrology, with a clean two-person credit, but the committee should decide whether to separate the clock from comb-related precedent.
responses.response: I agree with the ranking and think the separation holds. The 2005 citation concerned the comb as a ruler and optical frequency measurement; the lattice clock is a distinct step, because the magic-wavelength condition lets one interrogate many neutral atoms without motional shifts, and that is what gave the stability gain. I would nonetheless make the citation name the clock itself, not precision spectroscopy, so that it does not read as a repeat of 2005.

responses.point: B027 is a clean instrument-level invention in laser spectroscopy with independent confirmation at the 1e-18 level and no premature-confirmation concern; B032 atom interferometry is a strong measurement-science alternative.
responses.response: I share the maturity judgement. Where I qualify your view is on B032: it is substantial, but credit there is tangled by priority questions among early demonstrations and by Chu's earlier prize, while B027 has no comparable allocation problem. I would keep B032 as a later candidate and not combine it with the clock, since the three-person limit leaves no room for a fair second part.

responses.point: B041 IceCube opens a quantitative neutrino astronomy window and fits the discovery tradition of the prize, with Halzen and Karle as principal figures; B027 ranks second for him.
responses.response: I take the discovery argument seriously; a new observational window is exactly what the prize has honoured. My reservation is attribution. A cubic-kilometre collaboration with an AMANDA predecessor makes a two-name credit hard to defend, and the source identification is still developing. I would not oppose B041 on science, but I put it behind B027 until the credit question is better supported.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks redefined what a clock can do, with tests of relativity, variation of constants and dark matter, and a two-person prize looks fair; B057 is her second choice.
responses.response: I agree on the science and on the credit. On B057 I am more hesitant than you about timing: the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases, and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are missing from the credit, so the trio is defensible but not clean. I would keep it as a leading alternative if the clock stalls.

responses.point: B002 flocking founded the study of non-equilibrium collective order, but direct quantitative confirmation of the Toner-Tu exponents is thinner than the qualitative confirmation.
responses.response: I think that weak point is what holds B002 back for me. Qualitative confirmation in many systems is not a test of the specific scaling theory, and the Vicsek and Toner-Tu strands would be credited for different kinds of results. I do not rank it for this reason, though I respect the conceptual originality.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize.
Whether contributions from ion-clock groups and ultrastable-laser development weaken a two-name credit.
How close a circuit QED award would be to the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize, and whether Girvin and Devoret should be part of any such credit.
I cannot independently verify the detailed division of credit on any ballot beyond the supplied names.
statement.conflict_note: I am a professor at Chalmers and director of WACQT, with documented ties to colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and co-author Anton Frisk Kockum, and I work on circuit and waveguide QED. That is a possible recusal issue for B036 and for related superconducting-circuit candidates, and I note it as a reason to discount my own first-place opening support for B036. No specific connection to B027, Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile.
